You're right that "I am God" never appears verbatim on Jesus's lips, and I won't pretend otherwise — that's a real feature of the text, not a weakness to explain away. But the pattern of distinction you're pointing to is exactly what Trinitarian theology expects, not what it needs to explain away. Jesus is a distinct person from the Father — that's precisely why he prays to him, calls him "Father," and in John 17:3 speaks of him in the third person while addressing him. Distinction of persons is not division of essence. Notice, in that same John 17:3 context, Jesus has just asked the Father to glorify him with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed — hardly the language of a mere creature. And the very Gospel containing that prayer opens by declaring the Word was God and closes with Thomas's unrebuked confession, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28).

As for John 10:33 — the Jews weren't confused; they accused him of blasphemy for making himself God, and Jesus's reply appeals to Scripture to defend, not deny, the claim to a unique unity with the Father that provoked the charge in the first place. If Jesus were merely a distinct, lesser being, accepting worship — as he does from Thomas without correction — would itself be idolatry, forbidden absolutely by the Shema he was raised on: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The consistent New Testament pattern is not Jesus saying "I am the Father" — that would be modalism, not Trinitarian faith — but Jesus receiving what belongs to YHWH alone: the divine Name, divine titles, and divine worship, all while remaining, in his own person, the one who prays, obeys, and is sent. That is not a contradiction to square; it is the very shape of the Incarnation.

Jesus said many things about his authority, his unity with the Father, his pre-existence—but the direct statement "I am God" never appears on his lips in any Gospel.
